q: In the basic exam classification, primary memory consists of which two types?
explain: Primary memory is classified as RAM and ROM. HDD, SSD and optical discs are secondary storage.

q: Which of the following keeps its contents when the power is switched off?
explain: ROM is non-volatile. Conventional RAM, cache and registers are volatile and lose their contents without power.

q: Which of the following is an optical storage device?
explain: CD, DVD and Blu-ray are optical storage. HDD is magnetic, while SSD and pen drives are solid-state (flash).

q: Which statement correctly compares SRAM with DRAM?
options: SRAM is slower, denser and cheaper per bit
SRAM is faster, less dense and costlier per bit
SRAM needs periodic refresh while DRAM does not
SRAM is non-volatile while DRAM is volatile
explain: SRAM is generally faster but less dense and more expensive per bit, and it needs no refresh. Both SRAM and DRAM are volatile.

q: A conventional DRAM cell is made of which components?
options: A magnetic platter and a head
explain: A DRAM cell uses one transistor and one capacitor. The capacitor charge leaks, which is why DRAM needs periodic refresh.

q: Which memory type needs periodic refresh because its stored charge gradually leaks?
explain: DRAM (and its SDRAM forms) store bits as charge in capacitors and must be refreshed. SRAM does not need refresh while powered.

q: What is the full form of SDRAM?
explain: SDRAM is Synchronous Dynamic RAM, a DRAM subtype whose commands and transfers follow clock timing.

q: DDR SDRAM is called Double Data Rate because it transfers data on which clock edges?
options: Both the rising and falling edges
explain: DDR transfers data on both rising and falling clock edges. It is still a type of SDRAM.

q: Which memory type is commonly used to build processor cache?
explain: Cache needs speed, so it is commonly built from SRAM. DRAM, being denser and cheaper, is used for main memory.

q: Which statement about ROM is correct?
options: It is non-volatile and commonly stores firmware
It loses its data when power is removed
It is used as the main working memory for active programs
It cannot be called primary memory
explain: ROM keeps its contents after shutdown and commonly holds firmware. It is part of primary memory in the basic classification.

q: Which ROM type starts as a blank chip that can be programmed only once and not erased afterwards?
explain: PROM is programmable once by the user. Mask ROM is programmed at the factory, while EPROM and EEPROM can be erased.

q: How is a UV-erasable EPROM erased?
options: By ultraviolet light through a window in the package
explain: UV EPROM is cleared with ultraviolet light and then reprogrammed. Electrical erasure belongs to EEPROM.

q: Among the basic ROM types, which one is erased and rewritten electrically, commonly without removing the chip?
explain: EEPROM stands for Electrically Erasable Programmable ROM. Conventional EEPROM supports small, often byte-level updates.

q: What mainly distinguishes flash memory from conventional EEPROM?
options: Flash loses its data without power
Flash can be programmed only once
Flash is erased in blocks and offers higher density
Flash is erased with ultraviolet light
explain: Flash is electrically erased and rewritten in blocks, and this block erasure and density set it apart. It is non-volatile, and it is used in SSDs, USB drives and memory cards.

q: Device-control instructions stored in ROM or flash memory are known as what?
explain: Firmware is software that controls basic hardware functions, and it is stored in ROM or flash. Startup instructions were traditionally kept in ROM.

q: Which ROM type has its contents programmed during chip manufacture and cannot normally be changed afterwards?
explain: Mask ROM is programmed at manufacture. PROM is programmed once by the user later.

q: Which statement about CPU registers is correct?
options: Only registers exist inside a CPU
Conventional registers are volatile and faster to access than cache and RAM
Registers have the largest capacity of all memory
explain: Registers are tiny, fast and volatile. Modern CPUs also contain caches and internal buffers, so 'only registers' is too broad.

q: Which register temporarily holds the data that is moving to or from memory?
explain: MDR holds the data being transferred, while MAR holds the address of the memory location involved.

q: Accessing consecutive elements of an array is an example of which principle?
explain: Spatial locality means nearby memory locations are likely to be accessed soon, as with consecutive array elements.

q: Loop instructions that are executed again and again illustrate which principle?
explain: Temporal locality means recently used information is likely to be used again soon, as with instructions in a loop.

q: Which cache level is usually the smallest and fastest?
explain: L1 is usually the smallest and fastest, located within a core. L2 and L3 are generally larger but slower.

q: Which cache level is often shared by multiple cores and is frequently the last-level cache?
explain: L3 is often shared among several cores and is frequently the last-level cache, although the last level depends on the architecture.

q: Which statement about virtual memory is correct?
options: It physically increases the installed RAM
It is managed entirely by the hard disk
It is faster than physical RAM
It maps a virtual address space to physical memory, using disk backing when needed
explain: The OS maps virtual addresses to physical memory and may back some contents with HDD or SSD space. It does not add physical RAM, and disk-backed access is slower.

q: What is the term for excessive paging that leaves little time for useful computation and severely slows the system?
explain: Thrashing occurs when the system spends most of its time moving pages instead of doing useful work.

q: The disk area used to back virtual memory may be called what, depending on the operating system?
explain: The backing area is called swap space, a swap file or a page file. Virtual memory itself is broader than this disk area.

q: What is a group of 4 bits called?
explain: 4 bits make a nibble and 8 bits make a byte.

q: Which statement about kB and KiB is precisely correct?
options: Both kB and KiB are exactly 1,000 bytes
Both kB and KiB are exactly 1,024 bytes
explain: The binary unit KiB is 1,024 bytes and the decimal kB is 1,000 bytes. Older books often write 1 KB = 1,024, so follow the question's stated convention.

q: Which of these units is the largest?
explain: The order is terabyte (10^12), petabyte (10^15), exabyte (10^18), zettabyte (10^21) bytes.

q: Which of the following describes a data-transfer rate rather than a storage capacity?
explain: MB/s and GB/s measure transfer rate, while GB, TB and PB measure capacity. RPM measures platter rotation, not transfer rate.

q: In a hard disk drive, what does RPM measure?
explain: RPM is revolutions per minute of the platters (for example 5,400, 7,200 or 10,000). Total speed also depends on seek time, interface and workload.

q: In which year did IBM introduce the IBM 350 disk unit, the first commercial hard disk drive, as part of the IBM 305 RAMAC system?
explain: IBM introduced the IBM 350 Disk Storage Unit in 1956 with the IBM 305 RAMAC system.

q: Compared with a comparable HDD, which is generally true of an SSD that stores data in NAND flash?
options: It has spinning platters and is noisier
It has quicker access, quieter operation, lower power use and better shock resistance
explain: SSDs use NAND flash with no moving parts, so they are generally faster, quieter, lower in power use and more shock resistant. HDDs are magnetic and rated in RPM.

q: A pen drive (USB flash drive) retains data without power because it uses which technology?
explain: USB flash drives use non-volatile flash memory. They have no moving parts, so they resist mechanical shock better than HDDs.

q: Which pair of companies jointly developed the Compact Disc?
explain: The CD was developed jointly by Sony and Philips. Audio CDs launched in Japan in 1982 and Europe in 1983.

q: Which choice correctly gives the laser wavelength used for CD, DVD and Blu-ray respectively?
options: CD 650 nm, DVD 780 nm, BD 405 nm
CD 780 nm, DVD 650 nm, BD 405 nm
CD 405 nm, DVD 650 nm, BD 780 nm
CD 780 nm, DVD 405 nm, BD 650 nm
explain: CD uses a near-infrared laser of about 780 nm, DVD a red laser of about 650 nm and Blu-ray a blue-violet laser of about 405 nm. A shorter wavelength allows higher capacity.

q: Which disc type can be erased and recorded again with compatible equipment?
explain: CD-RW is Compact Disc Rewritable. CD-ROM is factory-recorded and CD-R recorded areas cannot be erased.

q: What is the capacity of a standard single-sided, single-layer DVD?
explain: A single-sided single-layer DVD holds 4.7 GB and a dual-layer one about 8.5 GB. 25 GB is a single-layer Blu-ray.

q: Which choice describes a standard single-layer Blu-ray disc?
options: 25 GB with a 650 nm red laser
25 GB with a 405 nm blue-violet laser
explain: A standard single-layer BD holds 25 GB and uses a blue-violet laser of about 405 nm (dual-layer holds 50 GB).

q: Who invented one-transistor DRAM, for which a patent was granted in 1968?
explain: Robert H. Dennard invented one-transistor DRAM (patent 1968). He did not invent both RAM and ROM.

q: Who is credited as the inventor of flash memory?
explain: Fujio Masuoka invented flash memory. Harari and Perlegos are linked with EEPROM, and Dennard with DRAM.
